description: We are a team of passionate engineering students interested in space, technology, and innovation. We aim to use our technical skills, creativity, and teamwork to develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges. Through NASA Space Apps Challenge, we hope to learn, collaborate, and turn our ideas into impactful projects.
summary:
🚀 Space Mission Challenge | NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026

Our project is an interactive educational game that combines space exploration, physics, engineering, and problem-solving.

Players embark on exciting space missions through different levels and challenges. Each level presents a unique mission that requires players to apply scientific laws, use mathematical formulas, perform calculations, and solve engineering problems to successfully complete their tasks.

Throughout the game, players can:
- Explore interactive 3D environments.
- Complete different space missions and challenges.
- Apply physics and engineering laws.
- Use formulas and scientific equations to solve problems.
- Perform calculations based on the given data.
- Overcome technical challenges and make decisions.
- Progress through increasingly challenging levels.

Our goal is to make learning science and engineering more engaging by turning theoretical knowledge into an interactive gaming experience.

Competition: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
Location: Cairo, Egypt

Thank you for watching! 🚀
details:
SpaceSync is a browser game that teaches space mission design by making players do the engineering. Its main mode, 3D Missions, has 25 levels in 5 sections: Rocket Science, Orbital Mechanics, Power & Thermal, Communications, and Planets & Landing. Each level is a separate mission with its own 3D scene, a written mission brief, its own reference laws (with variables and units) and 2–4 calculations.

How it works: the player reads the mission, explores the 3D scene and clicks markers on objects to collect the data (for example the rocket's mass, the engine thrust, or air density from a weather balloon), opens the Reference Laws tab, calculates each value and types it in. The game checks the answer against a value computed from the same data. Wrong answers are diagnosed without revealing the result (wrong unit or power of ten, ln vs log10, altitude instead of radius, a missing ½, forgetting gravity), and a hint showing the approach is available. Each correct answer moves the mission forward in 3D: the rocket lifts off, the spacecraft burns into GEO, the lander touches down. A second mode, Mission Designer, lets players buy parts, build a spacecraft within a budget and mass limit, and run a simulation that explains why it succeeded or failed.

Benefits and goal: students practise real mission-analysis skills (units, choosing the right law, margins, go/no-go decisions) and get specific feedback instead of a simple fail. It is free, works in any browser and offline as one HTML file, supports English and Arabic, and each mission takes 5–10 minutes, so it fits a class period.

Tools: JavaScript, HTML and CSS; a custom WebGL 3D renderer; an optional Node.js server; and Playwright for automated testing. All 25 levels were played end-to-end by automated tests.

Creativity: the player cannot win by guessing. The 3D world is only data until the player calculates, and the calculations drive the 3D story. Considerations: honest labelling (physical constants are real, scenario values are educational), no NASA logos, bilingual access, and low-end devices.

Status: working prototype. The 3D objects are simple shapes, profiles are saved on the device only, and the game has not yet been tested in a classroom.
